claim: Tobacco use is the leading cause of preventable death worldwide, with tobacco-related illnesses estimated to kill more than 6 million people annually.
source: It remains the leading cause of preventable death worldwide, with tobacco-related illnesses estimated to kill more than 6 million people annually (World Health Organization, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2011

claim: In the United States, the direct and indirect financial costs of smoking are estimated at more than $300 billion each year.
source: In the United States, the direct and indirect financial costs of smoking are estimated at more than $300 billion each year (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion, Office on Smoking and Health, 2014; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2014 and Xu et al., 2015

claim: A vast majority of all smokers begin smoking at age 18 or younger.
source: Adolescents are particularly at risk for initiating tobacco use, with a vast majority of all smokers beginning at age 18 or younger (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion, Office on Smoking and Health, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2014

claim: Adolescents are more susceptible than adults to the cellular and behavioral effects of nicotine.
source: A growing body of evidence from both human and animal studies indicates that adolescents are more susceptible than adults to the cellular and behavioral effects of nicotine, the main addictive component of tobacco (Adriani and Laviola, 2004; Counotte et al., 2011; Lydon et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Adriani and Laviola, 2004; Counotte et al., 2011; Lydon et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2015

claim: Nicotine modifies dopamine signaling in key regions of the brain's reward system.
source: Nicotine modifies dopamine (DA) signaling in key regions of the brain's reward system (Jasinska et al., 2014; De Biasi and Dani, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jasinska et al., 2014 and De Biasi and Dani, 2011

claim: Exposure to nicotine alters reward-related activity in dopaminergic reward regions in human smokers.
source: Human neuroimaging studies of smokers have shown that exposure to nicotine alters reward-related activity in dopaminergic reward regions (Rose et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rose et al., 2012

claim: Nicotine potentiates excitatory synaptic connections to DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) in rodents.
source: Moreover, in rodents, while nicotine is known to potentiate excitatory synaptic connections to DA neurons in the reward-related ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Mansvelder and McGehee, 2000; Saal et al., 2003), the precise molecular mechanism underlying nicotine-induced long-term potentiation (LTP) remains unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Mansvelder and McGehee, 2000 and Saal et al., 2003

claim: The precise molecular mechanism underlying nicotine-induced long-term potentiation (LTP) remains unclear.
source: Moreover, in rodents, while nicotine is known to potentiate excitatory synaptic connections to DA neurons in the reward-related ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Mansvelder and McGehee, 2000; Saal et al., 2003), the precise molecular mechanism underlying nicotine-induced long-term potentiation (LTP) remains unclear.
evidence: Stated as an explicit gap in knowledge

claim: The translation initiation factor eIF2α regulates adolescent vulnerability to the synaptic and behavioral effects of cocaine.
source: In a companion article (Huang et al., 2016), we found that the translation initiation factor eIF2α regulates adolescent vulnerability to the synaptic and behavioral effects of cocaine.
evidence: Supported by citation to companion article Huang et al., 2016

claim: Adolescent (5 weeks old) mice are more sensitive to a lower dose of cocaine than adult (3–5 months old) mice with regard to reduced phosphorylation of eIF2α, the induction of LTP, and cocaine-induced behavior.
source: Briefly, adolescent (5 weeks old) mice proved to be more sensitive to a lower dose of cocaine than adult (3–5 months old) mice with regard to reduced phosphorylation of eIF2α, the induction of LTP, and cocaine-induced behavior [conditioned place preference (CPP), a common behavioral task that reflects behavioral reinforcement underlying the development of drug addiction] (Koo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koo et al., 2012 and reference to companion article

claim: Genetic and pharmacological reduction in p-eIF2α-mediated translational control increases the susceptibility of adult mice to the synaptic and behavioral effects of cocaine.
source: Consistent with these findings, genetic and pharmacological reduction in p-eIF2α-mediated translational control increased the susceptibility of adult mice to the synaptic and behavioral effects of cocaine, making adult mice resemble adolescents in this respect.
evidence: Stated as findings from the companion study

claim: Drugs of abuse including nicotine that induce LTP in the VTA also reduce p-eIF2α in the VTA.
source: Furthermore, other drugs of abuse (including nicotine), that are known to induce LTP in the VTA (Saal et al., 2003), also reduced p-eIF2α in the VTA (Huang et al., 2016), thus highlighting the role of p-eIF2α as a common effector implicated in the initiation of addictive behavior.
evidence: Supported by citations to Saal et al., 2003 and Huang et al., 2016

claim: p-eIF2α is a common effector implicated in the initiation of addictive behavior.
source: Furthermore, other drugs of abuse (including nicotine), that are known to induce LTP in the VTA (Saal et al., 2003), also reduced p-eIF2α in the VTA (Huang et al., 2016), thus highlighting the role of p-eIF2α as a common effector implicated in the initiation of addictive behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the findings that multiple drugs of abuse reduce p-eIF2α and induce LTP

claim: A relatively low dose of nicotine (0.4 mg/kg i.p.) is sufficient to induce LTP in VTA DA neurons from adolescent mice, but not in adult mice.
source: We found that a relatively low dose of nicotine (0.4 mg/kg i.p.) was sufficient to induce LTP in VTA DA neurons from adolescent mice, but not in adult mice (Figure 1a, b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a, b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: A higher dose of nicotine (1.0 mg/kg) is required to elicit comparable LTP in VTA DA neurons from adult mice.
source: By contrast, a higher dose of nicotine (1.0 mg/kg) was required to elicit comparable LTP in VTA DA neurons from adult mice (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Nicotine induces LTP in VTA DA neurons at a significantly lower dose in adolescent mice compared to adult mice.
source: Thus, like cocaine, nicotine induces LTP in VTA DA neurons at a significantly lower dose in adolescent mice.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of nicotine doses required for LTP in adolescent vs. adult mice

claim: A low dose of cocaine reduces phosphorylation of eIF2α only in the VTA of adolescent mice.
source: In the accompanying article (Huang et al., 2016) we found that a low dose of cocaine reduces phosphorylation of eIF2α only in the VTA of adolescent mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to companion article Huang et al., 2016

claim: A low dose of nicotine (0.4 mg/kg) reduces p-eIF2α only in the VTA of adolescent mice.
source: Consistent with our findings with cocaine, we found that a low dose of nicotine (0.4 mg/kg) reduced p-eIF2α only in the VTA of adolescent mice (Figure 1c, d), whereas a higher dose of nicotine (1 mg/kg) was required to reduce p-eIF2α in the VTA of adult mice (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c, d

claim: A higher dose of nicotine (1 mg/kg) is required to reduce p-eIF2α in the VTA of adult mice.
source: Consistent with our findings with cocaine, we found that a low dose of nicotine (0.4 mg/kg) reduced p-eIF2α only in the VTA of adolescent mice (Figure 1c, d), whereas a higher dose of nicotine (1 mg/kg) was required to reduce p-eIF2α in the VTA of adult mice (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e

claim: Low doses of nicotine selectively reduce p-eIF2α in the VTA of adolescent mice.
source: Thus, like cocaine, low doses of nicotine selectively reduce p-eIF2α in the VTA of adolescent mice, highlighting the involvement of p-eIF2α-mediated translational control during this period of heightened vulnerability to the effects of drugs of abuse.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of nicotine effects on p-eIF2α in adolescent vs. adult mice

claim: p-eIF2α in VTA is reduced by about 50% in Eif2s1S/A mice because the phosphorylation site is mutated to alanine.
source: To test this prediction, we injected both adult control and Eif2s1S/A mice (in which p-eIF2α in VTA is reduced by about 50% because the phosphorylation site is mutated to alanine (Huang et al., 2016) with a low dose of nicotine (0.4 mg/kg i.p.).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2016

claim: A low dose of nicotine (0.4 mg/kg) does not typically induce LTP in adult wild-type mice.
source: This low dose does not typically induce LTP in adult wild-type (WT) mice (Figure 1b), and as expected, it failed to induce LTP in control WT Eif2s1S/S mice (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1f

claim: A low dose of nicotine (0.4 mg/kg) elicits LTP in adult Eif2s1S/A mice.
source: By contrast, the same low dose of nicotine elicited LTP in adult Eif2s1S/A mice (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f

claim: Adult mice with reduced eIF2α phosphorylation are more susceptible to the synaptic effects of nicotine.
source: Thus, like adolescent mice, adult mice with reduced eIF2α phosphorylation are more susceptible to the synaptic effects of nicotine.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that Eif2s1S/A mice show LTP with low dose nicotine

claim: ISRIB selectively blocks p-eIF2α-mediated translational control.
source: To further support these findings, we used the recently discovered small molecule ISRIB (Sidrauski et al., 2013), which selectively blocks p-eIF2α-mediated translational control (Sidrauski et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sidrauski et al., 2013

claim: A low dose of nicotine (0.4 mg/kg) induces LTP only in adult mice in which p-eIF2α-mediated translation is blocked pharmacologically with ISRIB.
source: Indeed, a low dose of nicotine (0.4 mg/kg) induced LTP only in adult mice in which p-eIF2α-mediated translation was blocked pharmacologically with ISRIB (Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g

claim: Adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translational control are more susceptible to nicotine-induced LTP.
source: Hence, like adolescent mice, adult mice with reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translational control are more susceptible to nicotine-induced LTP.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic and pharmacological experiments showing increased susceptibility to nicotine

claim: Reducing p-eIF2α-mediated translational control renders animals more susceptible to the effects of both cocaine and nicotine.
source: Thus, our findings that reducing p-eIF2α-mediated translational control renders animals more susceptible to the effects of both cocaine (Huang et al., 2016) and nicotine underscores a key role of p-eIF2α as a common regulator of drug-induced synaptic potentiation and behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the combined findings with cocaine and nicotine

claim: p-eIF2α is a common regulator of drug-induced synaptic potentiation and behavior.
source: Thus, our findings that reducing p-eIF2α-mediated translational control renders animals more susceptible to the effects of both cocaine (Huang et al., 2016) and nicotine underscores a key role of p-eIF2α as a common regulator of drug-induced synaptic potentiation and behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the findings that p-eIF2α regulates effects of multiple drugs of abuse

claim: Neuronal activity in key reward areas of the human brain is strongly associated with indices of drug use.
source: According to neuroimaging studies, neuronal activity in key reward areas of the human brain is strongly associated with indices of drug use (Rose et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rose et al., 2014

claim: The caudate and putamen are brain regions with crucial reward-related functional connections to the VTA.
source: We therefore measured reward-mediated activity in the caudate and putamen—brain regions with crucial reward-related functional connections to the VTA (Koob and Volkow, 2010)—of tobacco smokers and non-smokers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koob and Volkow, 2010

claim: Smokers show significantly lower reward-induced activity in the caudate and putamen compared to non-smokers.
source: Consistent with previous findings in cocaine and tobacco users (Rose et al., 2012; Rose et al., 2014), we observed significantly lower reward-induced activity in the caudate and putamen of smokers (Figure 2a and c), indicating that smokers find sweet drinks less rewarding.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and c, and citations to Rose et al., 2012 and Rose et al., 2014

claim: Smokers find sweet drinks less rewarding than non-smokers.
source: Consistent with previous findings in cocaine and tobacco users (Rose et al., 2012; Rose et al., 2014), we observed significantly lower reward-induced activity in the caudate and putamen of smokers (Figure 2a and c), indicating that smokers find sweet drinks less rewarding.
evidence: Inferred from the lower reward-induced brain activity in smokers

claim: The SNP rs10144417 in the Eif2s1 gene reveals an interaction between genotype and smoking status.
source: More importantly, we identified an SNP (rs10144417) in the Eif2s1 (eIF2α) gene that revealed an interaction between genotype and smoking status.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from fMRI study

claim: Smokers carrying the AG/GG genotype show lower reward-dependent activity compared with AA smokers.
source: While smokers carrying the AG/GG genotype showed lower reward-dependent activity compared with that of the AA smokers, such activity did not differ between non-smokers of both genotypes (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Reward-dependent activity does not differ between non-smokers of AA and AG/GG genotypes.
source: While smokers carrying the AG/GG genotype showed lower reward-dependent activity compared with that of the AA smokers, such activity did not differ between non-smokers of both genotypes (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d

claim: rs10144417 in the Eif2s1 gene is associated with both reward signaling and tobacco use.
source: These data indicate that rs10144417 in the Eif2s1 gene is associated with both reward signaling and tobacco use.
evidence: Inferred from the interaction between genotype and smoking status on reward activity

claim: rs10144417 spans a highly conserved region of the Eif2s1 promoter.
source: In silico analysis revealed that rs10144417 spans a highly conserved region of the Eif2s1 promoter (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by in silico analysis shown in Figure 2e

claim: The G variant of rs10144417 increases the transcriptional activity of the Eif2s1 promoter compared to the A variant.
source: We found that, compared to the A variant, the normalized G variant Fluc/Rluc ratio was significantly increased (~40%, Figure 2g), reflecting increased expression of Eif2s1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 2g

claim: Overexpression of Eif2s1 increases eIF2α levels.
source: Western blotting showing that overexpression of Eif2s1 (pRc/CMV-Eif2s1) increased eIF2α levels compared to control (vector alone pRc/CMV).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2h

claim: Increased expression of Eif2s1 significantly reduces translation of Ophn1 mRNA.
source: Strikingly, increased expression of Eif2s1 significantly reduced the normalized Fluc/Rluc ratio, indicating a significant reduction in translation of Ophn1 mRNA (Figure 2j).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 2j

claim: Expression of Eif2s1 selectively reduces 5'UTR-Ophn1-Fluc activity, but has no effect on Rluc activity.
source: Additionally, expression of Eif2s1 selectively reduced 5'UTR-Ophn1-Fluc activity, but had no effect on Rluc activity (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as experimental observation

claim: Overexpression of Eif2s1 reduces translation of a 5'UTR-Atf4 firefly luciferase reporter.
source: These data were further supported by our findings that overexpression of Eif2s1 also reduced translation of a 5'UTR-Atf4 firefly luciferase reporter (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), which is typically up-regulated by increased p-eIF2α (Sidrauski et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and citations

claim: Overexpression of the alpha subunit of eIF2 (Eif2s1) reduces p-eIF2α–mediated translation.
source: Hence, overexpression of the alpha subunit of eIF2 (Eif2s1) reduces p-eIF2α–mediated translation.
evidence: Inferred from the luciferase reporter assay results showing reduced translation of p-eIF2α-regulated mRNAs

claim: The mechanism by which increased expression of Eif2s1 inhibits p-eIF2α–mediated translation remains to be determined.
source: The mechanism by which increased expression of Eif2s1 inhibits p-eIF2α–mediated translation remains to be determined.
evidence: Stated as an explicit gap in knowledge

claim: Overexpression of Eif2s1 could affect eIF2α-mediated translation by altering the assembly of eIF2 complex.
source: Overexpression of Eif2s1 could affect eIF2α-mediated translation by altering: a) the assembly of eIF2 complex [eIF2 is a heterotrimer consisting of an alpha (encoded by Eif2s1), a beta (encoded by Eif2s2), and a gamma subunit (encoded by Eif2s3), b) the binding of eIF2 to key regulatory proteins (e.g., eIF2B and/or eIF5), or c) by titrating the phosphorylated alpha subunit away from the eIF2 complex.
evidence: Proposed as a possible mechanism

claim: Overexpression of Eif2s1 could affect eIF2α-mediated translation by altering the binding of eIF2 to key regulatory proteins.
source: Overexpression of Eif2s1 could affect eIF2α-mediated translation by altering: a) the assembly of eIF2 complex [eIF2 is a heterotrimer consisting of an alpha (encoded by Eif2s1), a beta (encoded by Eif2s2), and a gamma subunit (encoded by Eif2s3), b) the binding of eIF2 to key regulatory proteins (e.g., eIF2B and/or eIF5), or c) by titrating the phosphorylated alpha subunit away from the eIF2 complex.
evidence: Proposed as a possible mechanism

claim: Overexpression of Eif2s1 could affect eIF2α-mediated translation by titrating the phosphorylated alpha subunit away from the eIF2 complex.
source: Overexpression of Eif2s1 could affect eIF2α-mediated translation by altering: a) the assembly of eIF2 complex [eIF2 is a heterotrimer consisting of an alpha (encoded by Eif2s1), a beta (encoded by Eif2s2), and a gamma subunit (encoded by Eif2s3), b) the binding of eIF2 to key regulatory proteins (e.g., eIF2B and/or eIF5), or c) by titrating the phosphorylated alpha subunit away from the eIF2 complex.
evidence: Proposed as a possible mechanism

claim: Overexpression of Eif2s1 could alter the expression of a given eIF2α kinase or phosphatase.
source: Moreover, overexpression of Eif2s1 could alter the expression of a given eIF2α kinase or phosphatase.
evidence: Proposed as a possible mechanism

claim: Compensatory translational homeostatic mechanisms have been observed when the levels of key translation initiation factors are altered.
source: Such compensatory translational homeostatic mechanisms have been observed when the levels of key translation initiation factors (e.g., eIF4E, 4E-BPs, PABP, Paips) are either increased or decreased (Khaleghpour et al., 1999; Yanagiya et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Khaleghpour et al., 1999; Yanagiya et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2006

claim: Reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translational control mediates a genetic predisposition to greater risk for drug-induced changes in synaptic strength.
source: Collectively, our mouse and human data suggest that reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translational control mediates a genetic predisposition to greater risk for drug-induced changes in synaptic strength, which may account for the greater vulnerability of adolescents, even as first time drug users.
evidence: Inferred from the combined mouse and human findings

claim: Reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translational control may account for the greater vulnerability of adolescents to drugs of abuse.
source: Collectively, our mouse and human data suggest that reduced p-eIF2α-mediated translational control mediates a genetic predisposition to greater risk for drug-induced changes in synaptic strength, which may account for the greater vulnerability of adolescents, even as first time drug users.
evidence: Inferred from the combined mouse and human findings

claim: Mice with reduced eIF2α-mediated translation are more susceptible to nicotine-induced changes in synaptic function.
source: For instance, mice with reduced eIF2α-mediated translation are more susceptible to nicotine-induced changes in synaptic function.
evidence: Supported by the experimental findings with Eif2s1S/A mice and ISRIB treatment

claim: Smokers carrying the G variant show reduced reward-induced activity in the caudate and putamen.
source: Similarly, smokers carrying the G variant, who also have reduced eIF2α-mediated translation, show reduced reward-induced activity in the caudate and putamen, suggesting that such individuals are likely to consume more drugs to obtain reward activity comparable to that of non-smokers.
evidence: Supported by the fMRI data showing genotype-smoking interaction

claim: Smokers carrying the G variant have reduced eIF2α-mediated translation.
source: Similarly, smokers carrying the G variant, who also have reduced eIF2α-mediated translation, show reduced reward-induced activity in the caudate and putamen, suggesting that such individuals are likely to consume more drugs to obtain reward activity comparable to that of non-smokers.
evidence: Inferred from the luciferase assay showing G variant increases Eif2s1 expression, which reduces p-eIF2α-mediated translation

claim: Individuals carrying the G variant are likely to consume more drugs to obtain reward activity comparable to that of non-smokers.
source: Similarly, smokers carrying the G variant, who also have reduced eIF2α-mediated translation, show reduced reward-induced activity in the caudate and putamen, suggesting that such individuals are likely to consume more drugs to obtain reward activity comparable to that of non-smokers.
evidence: Speculated based on the reduced reward activity in G variant smokers

claim: These insights may hold promise for new p-eIF2α-based approaches to treating drug abuse.
source: Finally, these insights may hold promise for new p-eIF2α-based approaches to treating drug abuse.
evidence: Speculated based on the findings about p-eIF2α's role in drug susceptibility

claim: eIF2 is a heterotrimer consisting of an alpha subunit (encoded by Eif2s1), a beta subunit (encoded by Eif2s2), and a gamma subunit (encoded by Eif2s3).
source: Overexpression of Eif2s1 could affect eIF2α-mediated translation by altering: a) the assembly of eIF2 complex [eIF2 is a heterotrimer consisting of an alpha (encoded by Eif2s1), a beta (encoded by Eif2s2), and a gamma subunit (encoded by Eif2s3)
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about eIF2 structure

claim: Translation of Ophn1 mRNA is enhanced by conditions that increase p-eIF2α.
source: To determine whether overexpression of Eif2s1 could affect p-eIF2α–mediated translational control, we co-expressed in HEK293T cells Eif2s1 (Donzé et al., 1995) (Figure 2h), a 5'UTR-Ophn1 firefly luciferase reporter (5'UTR-Ophn1-Fluc; Figure 2i), whose translation is known to be enhanced by conditions that increase p-eIF2α (Di Prisco et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Di Prisco et al., 2014

claim: ATF4 is typically up-regulated by increased p-eIF2α.
source: These data were further supported by our findings that overexpression of Eif2s1 also reduced translation of a 5'UTR-Atf4 firefly luciferase reporter (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), which is typically up-regulated by increased p-eIF2α (Sidrauski et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sidrauski et al., 2013 and Lu et al., 2004

claim: An increase in the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio is an index of LTP.
source: An increase in this ratio was taken as an index of LTP.
evidence: Stated as an established method for measuring LTP

claim: Conditioned place preference (CPP) is a common behavioral task that reflects behavioral reinforcement underlying the development of drug addiction.
source: Briefly, adolescent (5 weeks old) mice proved to be more sensitive to a lower dose of cocaine than adult (3–5 months old) mice with regard to reduced phosphorylation of eIF2α, the induction of LTP, and cocaine-induced behavior [conditioned place preference (CPP), a common behavioral task that reflects behavioral reinforcement underlying the development of drug addiction] (Koo et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about CPP

claim: Nicotine is the principal addictive component driving tobacco smoking.
source: Adolescents are particularly vulnerable to nicotine, the principal addictive component driving tobacco smoking.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Nicotine is the main addictive component of tobacco.
source: A growing body of evidence from both human and animal studies indicates that adolescents are more susceptible than adults to the cellular and behavioral effects of nicotine, the main addictive component of tobacco (Adriani and Laviola, 2004; Counotte et al., 2011; Lydon et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge
